passage:
Teacher's note, Friday. At school pickup today I watched Ira, class 5, meet her grandfather at the gate. Just seconds earlier, in class, she had answered me in careful English: "Ma'am, I finished the worksheet." Then she saw Dadaji, ran up, and said in Bhojpuri, "Dadaji, hamar bag bhaari ba, tu utha ke chal!" He laughed and lifted it.
A classmate then asked her something in English, and she answered in English, and back to Bhojpuri for Dadaji, all in the same minute. Nobody had told her which language to use where. I noted it as an early skill: she reads the room.
Vishal, class teacher

qa.q: Which language did Ira use with her grandfather at the gate?
qa.a: Ira spoke Bhojpuri with Dadaji at the gate.

qa.q: What might Ira have been feeling when she saw Dadaji at the gate?
qa.a: Ira seems to have been happy and relaxed, since she ran up and spoke in the language of home. Her easy voice suggests she felt comfortable with him.

qa.q: What did Ira do that shows she chooses language by audience?
qa.a: Ira used careful English with the teacher and classmate and Bhojpuri with Dadaji, all in the same minute. She changed language to fit who she was talking to.

qa.q: How might Dadaji have felt when Ira spoke to him in Bhojpuri?
qa.a: Dadaji probably felt pleased and close to Ira, since he laughed and lifted the bag. Hearing his own language made him feel at home.

grounding: A child speaks a local dialect with a grandfather and English at school, sensing which fits where.

passage:
Sunday night. Today Simran came home with me after tuition. I was a bit nervous, because at home I talk in Hindi with Dadi, all the time, and Simran only talks English with me at school.
But when we got in, I said, "Dadi, ye Simran hai, meri friend," and Dadi gave her ladoo. Then I turned to Simran and said, "Try it, it's my Dadi's special." I did not even notice I was switching. Dadi asked me in Hindi what Simran liked, and I told Simran in English.
I liked being the bridge between them.
— Chetan

qa.q: Who came home with Chetan after tuition?
qa.a: Simran came home with Chetan after tuition.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on the way in, and how did it change?
qa.a: Chetan felt nervous at first about two worlds meeting. By the end Chetan felt proud and happy, liking being the bridge between Dadi and Simran.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that helped Dadi and Simran understand each other?
qa.a: Chetan spoke Hindi to Dadi and English to Simran, and passed on what each said. That way neither of them was left out.

qa.q: What might Simran have felt when Dadi gave her a ladoo?
qa.a: Simran probably felt welcomed and a little curious, since Dadi's Hindi was new to her. The ladoo showed kindness without needing words.

grounding: A child speaks Hindi with Dadi and English with a friend, sensing which fits where.

passage:
Monday. At breakfast, Leela spoke Bhojpuri with Dadi: "Dadi, roti mein ghee dal di?" Dadi smiled and gave her the bigger piece.
At school an hour later, in Mrs Fernandes's class, Leela put up her hand. "Ma'am, can I read the next paragraph?" Her classmate Darshan whispered, "You talk like two different people."
Wednesday. Darshan came over to do the project. Dadi asked him something in Bhojpuri, and he froze. Leela jumped in: "Dadi, he only knows Hindi and English." Then in Hindi to Darshan, "She's asking if you want tea."
Saturday. Leela went to the market with Dadi and switched again, bargaining for tomatoes in Bhojpuri. On the way back she said, "Dadi, at school I don't speak like this. Is that okay?"
Dadi patted her head. "You speak to people in the language that reaches them. That is cleverness."

qa.q: Which language did Leela speak with Dadi at breakfast?
qa.a: Leela spoke Bhojpuri with Dadi.

qa.q: Why did Leela ask Dadi if it was okay not to speak Bhojpuri at school?
qa.a: Leela felt a little unsure and worried that switching languages might seem disloyal to Dadi.

qa.q: How did Leela help when Darshan froze?
qa.a: She explained to Dadi that he only knew Hindi and English, then translated Dadi's question for him in Hindi.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Leela's language switching?
qa.a: At first Darshan finds it surprising, like two different people, but he is probably grateful when she translates for him at her home.

grounding: A child speaks Bhojpuri with a grandparent and English at school, sensing which language fits where.

passage:
"Deepika, you think switching languages is new? Sit, let me tell you about your Charu Nani at nine," she said, stirring her tea.
"My grandmother spoke only Konkani. At school, the nuns spoke English. With my friends on the street, we spoke Marathi. I was three different girls in one day.
"Once, the headmistress visited our house. My grandmother offered her a sweet in Konkani. The headmistress looked lost. I stood there, not knowing whether I was allowed to speak English at home. Then I said, 'Sister, she is saying please take one, they are fresh.' And to my grandmother in Konkani, 'She says thank you.'
"My grandmother pinched my cheek after. The headmistress praised me in class the next day.
"That was when I understood: every language has its own room, and I had keys to three.

qa.q: Which language did Charu Nani's grandmother speak?
qa.a: Her grandmother spoke only Konkani.

qa.q: What was young Charu feeling when the headmistress looked lost?
qa.a: Young Charu felt unsure and nervous, not knowing if she was allowed to speak English at home, before deciding to help.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: It was the moment young Charu chose to translate for both the headmistress and her grandmother, showing her she could move between languages to help people understand each other.

qa.q: How did Charu's grandmother feel about what happened?
qa.a: The grandmother was proud and pleased, pinching Charu's cheek after the visit.

grounding: An elder recalls speaking Konkani, English and Marathi as a child with different people, sensing which language fit where.

passage:
The wedding hall was so loud with drums that Reena had to shout. Her Nanaji, who spoke only Marwari, wanted to know where the dining area was. Her cousin Yogesh, visiting from London, spoke only English and was looking for the bathroom. And her mother had vanished into the crowd with the gift box.
Reena, ten, stood between them, turning from one to the other.
"Nanaji, khano upar hai, seedhi se," she said, pointing to the stairs.
Then to Yogesh: "Bathroom's behind the stage. Come, I'll show you."
Nanaji caught her arm. "Tu toh sabki bhasha bol leti hai."
Reena grinned and led Yogesh through the crowd, then came back and walked Nanaji up the stairs, holding his elbow.
When her mother finally appeared, Nanaji said, "Your daughter was our guide today."

qa.q: What was Yogesh looking for?
qa.a: Yogesh was looking for the bathroom.

qa.q: What was Reena likely feeling as she helped both relatives?
qa.a: Reena likely felt proud and capable, grinning when Nanaji praised her for speaking everyone's language.

qa.q: What could help a child like Reena in such a busy place?
qa.a: An adult could stay close or check in, so the child can help without feeling fully responsible for everyone.

qa.q: How did Nanaji see Reena's language switching?
qa.a: Nanaji was impressed and grateful, calling her their guide and saying she speaks everyone's language.

grounding: A child speaks Marwari with a grandparent and English with a cousin, sensing which language fits whom.

passage: Walking back from school through the Kankarbagh lanes, Anjali and Gopika argued in English about whose science model was taller. "Mine has a working fan, okay?" At Anjali's gate, Dadi sat on the steps shelling peas. Anjali's voice changed at once. "Ka ho Dadi, aaj ka banal ba?" she asked in Bhojpuri, dropping onto the step beside her. Dadi's face creased into a smile and she answered in a long, happy stream. Gopika stood a little lost. Anjali noticed, and said in slow Hindi, "Dadi, yeh Gopika hai. Iske model mein asli pankha hai." Dadi held out a handful of peas. Later Gopika asked how Anjali knew which language to use. Anjali shrugged. "Dadi words for Dadi. School words for school. The middle one when everyone's there."

qa.q: What was Dadi doing on the steps?
qa.a: Dadi sat on the steps shelling peas.

qa.q: How can you tell Anjali cared how Gopika felt at the gate?
qa.a: Anjali noticed Gopika standing a little lost and switched to slow Hindi to include her, wanting her to feel welcome.

qa.q: What small step could Anjali keep taking when people with different languages are together?
qa.a: Use the language everyone shares, like the slow Hindi at the gate, so nobody is left out.

qa.q: What was it like for Dadi when Anjali spoke Bhojpuri?
qa.a: Dadi's face creased into a smile and she chatted happily; hearing her own language from Anjali felt warm and close.

grounding: Shows a child switching between English with Gopika, Bhojpuri with a grandmother and Hindi for everyone, sensing which language fits where.
